a.q: A multi-tenant RAG service has 80 million chunks in an ANN index, with metadata for tenant, language and date. A query is restricted to one tenant that owns 1% of the chunks. The current code retrieves the top-10 vectors then drops those whose tenant does not match, and users often see 0-2 results. Explain why, compare post-filtering, pre-filtering and filter-aware ANN, and recommend a strategy as a function of filter selectivity.
a.answer:
Post-filtering (search first, filter afterwards) fails when the filter is selective: the global top-10 mostly belongs to other tenants. Oversampling, say fetching 1,000 candidates and then filtering, helps but is a guess, and the shortfall becomes unpredictable when the filter correlates with the query (a tenant's documents are typically about topics that other tenants' are not, or the reverse).

Pre-filtering (restrict to matching items, then search) returns the right number of results, but a naive ANN structure is built for the whole collection. If a graph (HNSW) is searched while skipping non-matching nodes, a restrictive filter can leave the traversal with few valid entry points or a disconnected valid subgraph, so recall may drop or latency may grow; behaviour is implementation-dependent, and engines add filter-aware traversal or fall back to other strategies. For IVF, filtering inside the probed lists is simple but wastes work scanning excluded vectors when the filter is restrictive (few vectors match).

Filter-aware ANN integrates the predicate into the search (traversing and collecting only valid nodes, or using per-filter indexes), which tends to be the best general approach if your engine supports it and you test its recall under the filters you actually use.

Strategy by selectivity: very selective filters (a tenant with, for example, tens of thousands of chunks) should not use the global ANN at all: use a per-tenant index/partition, or brute-force the matching set, which is exact and cheap at that size. Moderately selective filters: filter-aware ANN, verified against exact search. Loose filters (most data matches): post-filter with a modest oversampling factor plus a retry that doubles the candidate depth until k results are found or a limit is hit. Hard isolation requirements (security) are best met by separate partitions or enforced server-side filters, never by hoping that post-filtering is applied on every path.

b.q:
A 20M-chunk collection sits in an HNSW index. Queries always carry a metadata filter. For a filter such as department='legal' AND year=2019, only about 0.5% of vectors match (roughly 100,000 chunks). With ef_search=100 and top_k=10, the service often returns only 0 to 2 results, though the same query unfiltered returns 10 sensible hits and an exact scan with the filter returns 10 good ones.

Explain why this happens with post-filtering, what in-graph (filtered) traversal and pre-filtering change, and how you would choose a strategy by selectivity.
b.answer:
Post-filtering: the index returns the ef_search nearest candidates ignoring the filter, then the engine discards non-matching ones. If the filter is roughly independent of the query, the expected number of survivors is ef_search x selectivity = 100 x 0.005 = 0.5, far below top_k = 10. To get 10 survivors on average you would need ef around 2,000 (10 / 0.005), which costs latency and still fails when the filter correlates with the query (a query about a topic that lies mostly outside 'legal 2019' will rarely have matching items among its nearest neighbours). Raising top_k does not help for the same reason.

Pre-filtering with exact scan: evaluate the filter first (inverted index or bitmap), giving about 100,000 ids, then compute exact distances for just those. For 768-d float32 vectors that is about 100,000 x 768 x 4 bytes = 307 MB of vector data to read, acceptable for a rare query pattern and perfect recall within the filter, but too heavy at high QPS or when the filter passes millions of vectors.

Traversal-time (in-graph) filtering: search the graph but only admit matching nodes to the result set, in some engines still walking through non-matching nodes and in others restricting the walk to matching ones. It works well for moderate selectivity, but when matching nodes are very sparse, the search wanders through mostly non-matching regions, the effective graph of matching nodes can become disconnected, and recall or latency degrades; implementations differ in how they handle this (for example by switching to a brute-force path when the filter is selective enough).

Partitioning: if a few filter fields are used on nearly every query (tenant, year, language), build separate indexes or partitions per value so that the ANN index only holds eligible vectors.

Choosing: estimate selectivity per query from filter statistics; use post-filter with generous ef when most data matches (for example more than half); use traversal-time filtering in the middle range; use pre-filter plus exact scan when the matching set is small enough to scan within the latency budget. Always measure recall against an exact filtered search on a sample of real filter/query combinations, split by selectivity band, since average recall hides the selective cases.

a.q: A nightly retraining DAG runs ingest -> validate -> build_features -> train -> evaluate -> register. After a transient failure in train, the orchestrator retried the whole run from build_features. The next morning the feature table has duplicated rows for 3 days, two models are registered under the same version tag, and a colleague's backfill of last week's partitions produced different features than the originals. List the design faults and how you would fix each, including how a step's cache key should be formed.
a.answer:
Each symptom points to a step that is not idempotent, or to an ambiguous identity of inputs.

1. Duplicated rows after a retry: build_features appended to the table. A retried step must produce the same final state as a single successful run. Fix: write by partition key with overwrite or upsert (replace partition for date D), or write to a temporary location and atomically swap or commit on success, so a partial first attempt is discarded.
2. Two models with the same version tag: register created a new entry with a caller-chosen name. Fix: derive identity from content or run (training run id plus input hashes), make registration idempotent (registering the same run twice returns the same version), and never let a step overwrite an existing version.
3. Backfill produced different features: the step read something that is not a pure function of the partition: 'now', 'latest' reference tables, current code, or an unpinned join. Fix: pass the logical date as an explicit parameter; read versioned or as-of snapshots of reference data; pin code and environment versions; record them in the step's outputs.
4. Retry granularity: restarting the whole run repeats successful steps. Fix: persist each step's output as an artifact addressed by its inputs, and let a retry resume from the failed step; cap retries and use backoff for transient errors, but fail fast on deterministic ones (a schema violation will fail identically every time).
5. Failed attempts left partial artifacts behind (a half-written feature partition, a stored but unregistered model) that later attempts could pick up. Fix: write to a temporary location, commit or rename only on success, and let downstream steps read only committed outputs.

Cache key: a step's output can be reused only if everything that influences it is unchanged. So the key is a hash of (step name, code version or hash of the step's code and its dependencies, parameters, and the content hashes of every input artifact), using a canonical serialisation (sorted keys). Do not include volatile values such as wall-clock time. Unhashable hidden inputs (an external table read by name, an unpinned model download) break caching correctness, so they must be turned into explicit versioned inputs.

b.q: A nightly ML pipeline runs five steps as containerised jobs: extract, build_features, train, evaluate, register_model. Two incidents occurred this week. First, train was OOM-killed at 90% and retried automatically; register_model then ran twice for that day and created two registry versions with identical weights. Second, a retried build_features step overwrote its output directory while train was starting, and train read a half-written dataset without error. Explain what properties each step needs, how you would pass artifacts between steps, and where caching and retries fit.

Root cause: orchestrators and job controllers give at-least-once execution. Kubernetes documents that for Jobs the same program may sometimes be started twice, so a step must tolerate duplicate runs. So each step has to be safe to run more than once and safe to be observed mid-run.

Properties each step needs. (1) Idempotent: running it again with the same inputs yields the same outcome and no duplicate side effects. register_model is the offender in the first incident; make it a get-or-create keyed by an idempotency key such as the training run id or the model artifact hash, so a second attempt finds the existing version and returns it. (2) Atomic publication of outputs: build_features should write to a temporary location unique to the attempt and publish only at the end (an atomic rename where the filesystem guarantees it, or, on object stores without atomic directory rename, a completion marker such as a manifest listing files and checksums). Downstream steps read only complete, marked outputs. That removes the half-written read in the second incident, and it works because train is told which committed output to read, rather than listing a directory that something else may still be writing. Passing artifacts. Steps exchange references, not large payloads: a URI plus checksum (and schema version) stored by the orchestrator, with the artifact in object or shared storage. The downstream step verifies the checksum before use, which catches truncation.

a.q: A teammate argues: 'We already save every trained model into a versioned folder in object storage, so a model registry is redundant.' What does a registry add beyond that folder, and in what situation would the folder genuinely be enough?
a.answer:
A registry turns 'a file somewhere' into a managed, addressable model with history. The folder gives you bytes with a naming convention; a registry typically adds:

1. Version identity. Each registration under a model name gets a new, immutable version number (MLflow's registry documents the incrementing version number; treating a version as immutable is the intended usage rather than something that page spells out), so 'model X v12' means one specific artifact.
2. Lineage. Each version links back to what produced it: the training run, code commit, data snapshot and config, so you can answer 'how was the model in production built?'
3. Metadata. Tags, descriptions, evaluation results and the input/output signature travel with the version, so a consumer can validate requests without opening the artifact.
4. Named pointers. Consumers ask for 'production' (an alias or stage) instead of a path. Promotion and rollback become re-pointing that name, and a registry with auditing enabled can record who moved it and when. MLflow documents aliases as mutable named references to a version.
5. Governance. Access control, approvals and an audit trail around who may promote.

The folder is genuinely enough when there is one model, one author and one consumer, nothing is promoted through environments, and nobody will ever ask for provenance. Even then, the convention you invent (latest, final, v2) tends to be a hand-built registry with fewer guarantees.

Pitfall: a registry does not create reproducibility on its own. If the training job does not log the data version, seeds and environment, the lineage field is empty or misleading.

b.q: Auditors ask you to bring back, with behaviour equivalent to the original, the model that served customers 14 months ago, and to show how it was built. Design what each registry version must record and how the model is packaged, then describe how promotion and rollback should work using aliases, including what is and is not atomic.
b.answer:
Record per version (immutable once registered):
- Artifact in the chosen format with a content digest, plus the preprocessing it depends on, packaged inside it or versioned and referenced explicitly.
- Lineage: training run, code commit, data snapshot identifier or hash, configuration, seeds, and the feature definitions' version. MLflow's registry documents linking a version to the run that produced it, which is the pattern to copy.
- Signature, evaluation results against the baseline, who approved the promotion.
- Environment: dependency lockfile with hashes, base image referenced by digest (tags are mutable), hardware class.

Equivalent behaviour needs more than the weights: if the feature pipeline or an encoder lives outside the artifact, the old version of that code must also be recoverable. Exact bit-for-bit equality can be unrealistic across hardware, so define 'equivalent' as agreement within a stated tolerance on a replay set.

Aliases. Versions should never change (treat them as immutable by convention); aliases (for example 'production') are mutable named pointers, which MLflow documents. Promotion moves the alias from v39 to v41. A single alias update is one registry write (atomic in typical database-backed registries; MLflow's documentation does not state this), but running replicas do not notice unless they re-resolve it. A safe pattern is to resolve the alias to an explicit version when you create the deployment, and record that version, not the alias, in the deployment record. Rollback is then the same operation in reverse (alias back to v39, redeploy v39), which only works if v39's artifact and image are still retained. Retention policy is therefore part of the design: cleanup jobs that delete 'old' images silently destroy your ability to roll back or to answer an audit.

a.q: Implement single-head causal self-attention decoding two ways in numpy: class Decoder(Wq, Wk, Wv, use_cache) with step(x) taking the newest token embedding (d_model,) and returning its attention output, either re-projecting the whole prefix every step (use_cache=False) or storing past keys and values and projecting only the new token (use_cache=True). Show that both equal a full causal-masked attention pass (full_causal_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv)), count how many K/V rows each approach projects for T tokens, and write kv_cache_bytes(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch, bytes_per_elem). Example: 32 layers, 32 KV heads of size 128, fp16, 4096 tokens, batch 1 needs 2 GiB. Explain where the saving comes from and how cache memory grows.

```python
import numpy as np


class Decoder:
    """Single-head causal self-attention decoded one token at a time."""

    def __init__(self, Wq, Wk, Wv, use_cache):
        self.Wq, self.Wk, self.Wv = Wq, Wk, Wv
        self.use_cache = use_cache
        self.K = np.zeros((0, Wk.shape[1]))     # cached keys   (t, d)
        self.V = np.zeros((0, Wv.shape[1]))     # cached values (t, d)
        self.history = np.zeros((0, Wq.shape[0]))
        self.kv_rows_projected = 0              # how many K/V rows we had to compute

    def step(self, x):
        """x: (d_model,) embedding of the newest token. Returns attention output (d,)."""
        q = x @ self.Wq
        if self.use_cache:
            self.K = np.vstack([self.K, x @ self.Wk])    # project ONLY the new token
            self.V = np.vstack([self.V, x @ self.Wv])
            self.kv_rows_projected += 1
            K, V = self.K, self.V
        else:
            self.history = np.vstack([self.history, x])
            K = self.history @ self.Wk                   # re-project the whole prefix
            V = self.history @ self.Wv
            self.kv_rows_projected += len(self.history)
        s = K @ q / np.sqrt(len(q))                      # the newest token attends to 0..t (causal by construction)
        w = np.exp(s - s.max())
        w /= w.sum()
        return w @ V


def full_causal_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    """Reference: all positions at once with a causal mask (what training does)."""
    q, k, v = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(q.shape[1])
    s = np.where(np.tril(np.ones_like(s)) > 0, s, -np.inf)
    w = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True))
    w /= w.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ v


def kv_cache_bytes(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_elem=2):
    return 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_elem   # 2 = keys and values
```

b.q:
A team hosting a decoder-only model wants a small capacity-planning helper. Write two functions.

kv_cache_bytes(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_elem=2) returns the bytes needed to cache keys and values for `batch` sequences of `seq_len` tokens.

max_concurrent_sequences(total_bytes, weight_bytes, reserve_bytes, n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, bytes_per_elem=2) returns how many full-length sequences fit after subtracting the weights and a fixed reserve (activations, runtime overhead) from the device memory. It returns 0 if not even one fits, and raises ValueError if weights plus reserve already exceed total memory.

Validate inputs: every size must be an int (bool and float rejected with TypeError) and positive (ValueError); reserve_bytes may be 0. Then, for a hypothetical 32-layer model with head_dim 128, 4,096-token sequences, an fp16 cache, an 80 GiB device, 14e9 bytes of weights and a 6 GiB reserve, report how many sequences fit with 32 KV heads versus 8 KV heads, and what that tells you about the design of the attention layer.
b.answer:
The cache stores one key vector and one value vector per layer, per KV head, per token, so bytes = 2 x n_layers x n_kv_heads x head_dim x seq_len x batch x bytes_per_elem. It is linear in every factor, which is why, for a model this size with long contexts and large batches, the cache rather than the weights is what exhausts memory.

For the hypothetical model: per token the cache is 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 bytes (0.5 MiB) with 32 KV heads, so a 4,096-token sequence needs exactly 2 GiB. With 8 KV heads it is 128 KiB per token and 512 MiB per sequence.

Capacity: usable = 80 GiB - 14e9 bytes (about 13.04 GiB) - 6 GiB, roughly 60.96 GiB. Floor division by 2 GiB gives 30 sequences with 32 KV heads; dividing by 512 MiB gives 121 with 8 KV heads. At 1,024 tokens the 8-head model would hold 487.

What it tells you: the number of KV heads is a direct lever on concurrency. Multi-query and grouped-query attention share each key/value head across several query heads, which shrinks the cache and, per the GQA paper, is aimed at faster decoder inference while staying close to multi-head quality after uptraining. The trade-off is an architectural choice that must be made at training (or uptraining) time, and quality should be checked.

Pitfalls: the formula is an optimistic estimate. Real servers also lose memory to fragmentation, to activations, and to allocation granularity, and they may share prefix blocks between requests, so treat the result as a planning bound. Also state your units (GiB vs GB) and the cache dtype, which can differ from the weight dtype.

a.q: Your team logs every training run to an experiment tracker and also keeps a model registry. A new hire asks why one of them is not enough. What belongs in each, and how would you answer 'which code, data and run produced the model that is serving traffic right now?'
a.answer:
Different jobs, different lifecycles.

Experiment tracker: high volume, mostly disposable. For each run it stores parameters, metrics over time, tags, evaluation plots and output artifacts, plus the identity of the inputs (code commit, data snapshot id, config, seeds, environment). MLflow Tracking, for instance, describes logging parameters, code versions, metrics and output files, with a run holding metadata and artifacts. Use it to compare, filter and debug experiments; runs that never get promoted are still valuable evidence of what was tried.

Model registry: low volume, governed. It stores promoted model versions as entries that should be treated as immutable, with a name, a version number, a movable pointer (alias or stage) such as 'candidate' or 'production', the input/output signature, the validation results that justified promotion, who approved it, and a reference to the training run. The pointer move is the deployment-relevant event, and it can be audited and reversed. A plain file bucket typically has none of this by default: no enforced immutability (unless object lock or versioning is configured and used consistently), no pointer semantics, no approval trail, no link to evidence.

Answering the serving question is a chain of links, and every link must be recorded: (1) the serving process logs the model version it loaded (and the artifact checksum) with each prediction or at least at start-up; (2) the registry entry for that version points to the training run; (3) the run holds the commit hash, the data snapshot hash, the config, the seeds, and the environment (lockfile hash, image digest). If any link is only a convention ('the file name has the date'), lineage breaks the first time someone copies a file by hand.

Pitfalls: registering a model without the preprocessing/fitted artifacts it needs; promoting by overwriting a file in place so that the version number no longer identifies bytes; and logging the run id in the tracker but not carrying it into the registry or into the serving logs.

a.q: You are choosing among a 384-d, 768-d and 1,024-d embedding model for 20 million chunks, and the vector index must fit in a 64 GB node (with some headroom for the OS, metadata and query processing). Do the memory arithmetic for float32, float16 and int8 storage, add the graph overhead for HNSW with M = 16, and explain which options fit and what you would do beyond arithmetic to decide.
a.answer:
Raw storage is N x d x bytes_per_value (decimal GB): 20M x 384 x 4 B = 30.72 GB; 20M x 768 x 4 B = 61.44 GB; 20M x 1,024 x 4 B = 81.92 GB. Halving the precision halves these: the 1,024-d model is 40.96 GB in float16 and 20.48 GB in int8. HNSW with M = 16 stores up to 2M = 32 neighbour links at layer 0, each 4 B, so about 128 B/vector, i.e. roughly 2.56 GB for 20M vectors (upper layers add a small fraction, and exact overhead depends on the library).

What fits in 64 GB (with links): everything except 768-d float32 (about 64 GB, no headroom) and 1,024-d float32 (about 84.5 GB). The notable ones are 384-d float32 (about 33 GB), 768-d float16 (about 33 GB), 1,024-d float16 (about 43.5 GB) and 1,024-d int8 (about 23 GB); 384-d float16/int8 and 768-d int8 need only about 10-18 GB. Also remember ids, chunk metadata, replicas, a build phase that can need extra memory, and the fact that serving needs headroom, so treat 64 GB as about 45-50 GB of usable index, which makes 1,024-d float16 tight and the others comfortable.

Beyond arithmetic: dimension does not decide quality. Evaluate each model on your own labelled queries (recall@k or nDCG), then evaluate the compression you would apply (float16 usually costs little accuracy (FAISS notes some precision loss is possible, so measure it); int8 and PQ cost some recall, which you measure and may recover by re-ranking with full vectors from disk). Some models are trained so that truncating the vector to a prefix still works; use that only when the model documentation states it, and check quality. Finally weigh embedding cost and query latency, which also scale with dimension.

b.q: You must serve 50 million chunks, 768-d float32 embeddings, from an in-memory HNSW index with M=16, with 3 replicas for availability and throughput. Each node has about 100 GB usable for the index. Estimate memory for the base design, work out how many nodes it needs, and compare it with int8 scalar quantisation and product quantisation with 96-byte codes. Which would you choose and what would you verify before deciding?
b.answer:
Assumptions (state them in the interview; real engines differ): decimal GB; layer 0 stores up to 2M = 32 neighbour ids of 4 bytes per node; upper layers add roughly n/(M-1) node-layer entries with up to M links each; per-node headers, ids, allocator overhead and metadata are ignored and typically add more.

Base design: vectors = 50e6 x 768 x 4 B = 153.6 GB. Layer-0 links = 50e6 x 32 x 4 B = 6.4 GB. Upper layers add about 0.2 GB. Total about 160.2 GB per full copy. Three replicas = about 480.6 GB cluster-wide.

Nodes: one copy does not fit within 100 GB, so shard it: ceil(160.2 / 100) = 2 shards of about 80 GB each, times 3 replicas = 6 nodes. Replicas multiply cost but not capacity.

int8 scalar quantisation: 1 byte per dimension gives 38.4 GB for vectors plus 6.6 GB for the graph = 45.0 GB per copy, which fits on one node, so 3 nodes with 3 replicas. The recall loss is often small but data- and model-dependent, so measure it.

Product quantisation with 96 one-byte codes per vector (8 dimensions per sub-vector): 4.8 GB + 6.6 GB = 11.4 GB per copy. Each copy fits on one node, so it still needs 3 nodes (the replica count is the floor), the same as int8; the gain is only that nodes could be much smaller. It is lossy: distances are approximate, so many setups re-rank the top candidates with full-precision vectors stored on SSD or in object storage (153.6 GB on disk), adding latency and I/O. The graph links, not the vectors, dominate once codes are this small.

Decision: with these assumptions, int8 gets from 6 nodes to 3 and is a reasonable first step; PQ pays off when memory is the binding constraint. Before deciding, compare recall@k and end-to-end answer quality against the float32 index on a real query set, measure latency under load at the intended QPS and ef_search, and check the build and rebuild time and cost, since sharded indexes also need a fan-out and merge of per-shard top-k results.
