b.q:
A RAG bot is asked: 'How many days of notice are needed to cancel the contract?' The retriever returns only a superseded policy page saying 30 days (the current policy says 60). Three candidate answers:

A: 'You need 30 days of notice.'
B: 'You need 60 days of notice.' (no retrieved text mentions 60)
C: 'Cancellations must be made in writing and follow the contract terms.'

For each answer say whether it is faithful, relevant and correct, state which inputs each of those three judgements needs, and explain what this implies for choosing the headline metric of a RAG evaluation.
b.answer:
Faithfulness (groundedness): are the claims in the answer supported by the retrieved context? Inputs: answer and context only. Answer relevance: does the answer address the question asked? Inputs: question and answer. Correctness: does it match the truth? Inputs: a reference answer or an authoritative source.

A: faithful (30 days is in the context), relevant, incorrect. The generator did its job; the failure is upstream, in retrieval or in index freshness (a superseded document outranked or replaced the current one). Faithfulness scoring alone would give this answer full marks.

B: unfaithful (60 is not in the retrieved text), relevant, correct. Perhaps the model recalled it from pre-training or guessed. It looks good on a correctness metric but is untrustworthy: on another question the same behaviour yields confident fabrications. A strict grounded-answer product would count this as a failure even though the user got the right number.

C: only loosely relevant (on-topic but non-responsive) and not correct. Its faithfulness depends on text we are not shown: if the retrieved page really says cancellations must be in writing under the contract terms it is faithful, otherwise it is unsupported too. When supported, it is the typical 'safe vague' answer that high faithfulness scores reward. Relevance and correctness catch it.

Implications: no single number is enough. Faithfulness guards against unsupported claims but not against bad context; correctness needs labelled references, which are expensive and go stale when policies change; relevance is cheap but weak. Report them together and read the pattern: low faithfulness points at generation (prompting, decoding, instruction to abstain), faithful-but-wrong points at retrieval, freshness or the corpus, and relevant-but-vague points at prompt or answer-format issues. Also check context relevance/recall separately, since an LLM judge of faithfulness inherits any errors in the context it is shown.

a.q: Your RAG team splits every document into 512-token chunks with no overlap and gets noticeably worse answers on questions whose answer straddles a paragraph boundary. A colleague says 'just raise the overlap to 128'. Estimate what that does to index size for a 10,000-token document, and describe how you would decide on chunk size and overlap using retrieval measurements rather than intuition.
a.answer:
Overlap repeats the last o tokens of one chunk at the start of the next, so a sentence cut at a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk. With chunk size s and overlap o the stride is s - o, the chunk count for a document of L tokens is 1 + ceil((L - s) / (s - o)), and total stored tokens are about L + (chunks - 1) * o. For L = 10,000 and s = 512: o = 0 gives 20 chunks (10,000 tokens); o = 64 gives 23 chunks (about 11,400 tokens, +14%); o = 128 gives 26 chunks (about 13,200 tokens, +32%). Embedding cost, vector memory and index size scale with those counts.

Costs beyond storage: neighbouring chunks now contain the same text, so one relevant passage can occupy several of the top-k slots, wasting context budget unless you deduplicate or merge adjacent hits. Overlap is also a blunt fix: it only rescues answers shorter than the overlap, and it does nothing when the answer needs a heading or table header that lives far away. Splitting on structure (sentences, paragraphs, headings) usually removes more boundary damage than blind overlap.

Chunk size itself is a trade-off: small chunks give precise embeddings and cheap context but lose surrounding meaning and raise the number of vectors; large chunks keep context but blur several topics into one vector and consume prompt tokens. There is no universal best value; it depends on the corpus, the embedding model's input behaviour and the question types (lookup versus synthesis).

So decide empirically: build a labelled query set where each query has the answer-bearing text span marked, re-chunk the corpus under each setting, and score retrieval by whether a retrieved chunk contains the span (recall@k, MRR), because chunk IDs change between configurations. Then check end-to-end answer quality on a sample, since a retrieval gain can vanish once duplicates crowd the prompt.

b.q: After a weekend re-index in which you also switched to a newer embedding model and changed chunk size from 512 to 256, answer quality drops and some previously working queries now fail. Without being able to blame one change by intuition, how do you isolate the cause, and what would you have done before the migration to make this easy?
b.answer:
Three changes were made at once: embedding model, chunk size, and (implicitly) a full re-ingest that may have altered parsing, filters or metadata. Isolate by changing one factor at a time against a fixed labelled query set, and do not rely on intuition about which factor is likely.

Isolation procedure:
1. Reproduce with a regression set: take queries that worked before (from logs or the golden set) and measure recall@k and answer quality on the old and new index. Identify the queries that regressed; patterns (long queries, identifiers, tables) hint at the cause.
2. Build a factor grid if the old index is still available: old model with 512 chunks (baseline), new model with 512, old model with 256, new model with 256. Compare each against baseline, scoring hits by whether a retrieved chunk contains the labelled answer span (chunk IDs differ across chunk sizes), and keep in mind that the same k covers half as much text at 256 tokens. Interactions matter too, and the new model may need a different query/document prefix or normalisation, and the embedding dimension or similarity metric may differ.
3. Check for plain bugs unrelated to the factors: query and document embedded by different model versions (a mixed index or an unchanged query encoder), wrong distance metric for the new model, missing normalisation, lost metadata fields so filters match nothing, a truncated input exceeding the new model's token limit, different parsing, or an incomplete index (count of chunks versus expectation).
4. Chunk size effect on the prompt: 256-token chunks double the chunk count per document, so the same top-k now covers half the text; if k and the context budget were not retuned, the model sees less evidence per query.
5. Verify end-to-end separately from retrieval, since a retrieval gain can still reduce answer quality.

Prevention: version the index (blue/green with an alias), keep the old index until the new one passes the regression set, change one thing per release, keep a frozen canary query set with expected sources, and log the model and chunker versions in the chunk metadata. Rolling back then takes one alias flip back to the old collection (alias changes are atomic), provided the old collection was kept.

a.q:
Implement four retrieval-evaluation functions in plain Python (no libraries):

recall_at_k(ranked, relevant, k) -> float
reciprocal_rank(ranked, relevant) -> float, and mrr(runs) for runs = [(ranked, relevant), ...]
ndcg_at_k(ranked, gains, k, exponential=False) -> float, where gains = {doc: graded relevance >= 0}, DCG = sum g_i / log2(i+1) with g = rel (or 2**rel - 1 if exponential), and the ideal ranking is built from all judged documents.

Conventions to implement: ranked lists may contain duplicates (drop every repeat after a document's first occurrence before ranking, so later documents move up one position per dropped repeat); a query with no relevant documents scores 0.0; unjudged documents count as non-relevant.

Example: ranked = ['d3','d1','d7','d2','d5'], relevant = {'d1','d2','d9'}, gains = {'d1': 3, 'd2': 2, 'd9': 1}. recall@3 = 1/3, recall@5 = 2/3, RR = 0.5, nDCG@5 = 0.578 (linear gain) or 0.608 (exponential gain).

Then say what each metric hides.

b.q: Your retrieval golden set was built by annotators who judged only the top 10 results of the existing BM25 system for each query. You now evaluate a new dense retriever against it: its recall@10 and nDCG@10 come out lower than BM25's, yet when you read its results for 20 queries by hand, they look as good or better. Why can the metrics say this, and how would you fix the evaluation?
b.answer:
Recall, precision and nDCG all treat a document as relevant only if it appears in the judged-relevant set; unjudged documents count as non-relevant. When the labelled set came from the top 10 of BM25 only, relevant documents that BM25 cannot find were never shown to annotators, so they have no label. A dense retriever that surfaces such documents is penalised for exactly the behaviour you want, while BM25 is flattered because its own top results are the ones that got judged. This is pooling bias, and the metrics are biased towards systems similar to the one that built the pool.

Small example: the labelled relevant set for a query is {d1, d2, d3}. The dense system returns [d1, x, y, d2, z]. If x and y are truly relevant but never judged, measured recall@5 is 2/3 and precision@5 is 2/5, while the real precision@5 is 4/5 (if z is not relevant).

Diagnose it by computing the judged fraction at k (the share of each system's top-k that has any label). If BM25 is near 100% and the dense system is much lower, the comparison is unreliable. Also sample the unjudged dense results and have a human (or a carefully validated LLM judge) label them to estimate how many are relevant.

Fixes: (1) pool the top results from several different systems (BM25, dense, hybrid, the new candidate) before annotating, and re-pool when you add a new system; (2) judge the unjudged documents in the new system's top k, which is usually a small extra batch; (3) as a sensitivity check, report metrics on 'condensed lists' that drop unjudged documents; (4) keep the judged fraction as a standard column in every eval report; (5) when labels are partial, treat measured precision@k as a lower bound (unjudged hits count as misses); measured recall is biased too, but its denominator is also incomplete, so it is not a strict bound. More queries do not help because the missing labels bias every query in the same direction.

a.q:
You use an LLM judge to label RAG answers as 'ok' (faithful to the retrieved context) or 'bad'. On 100 answers a human reviewer also labelled, the two agree on 91. The human marked 90 answers ok and 10 bad; the judge marked 95 ok and 5 bad. A colleague says 'it agrees 91% of the time, so we can trust it as our faithfulness gate'.

Reconstruct the confusion matrix, compute Cohen's kappa, and explain why the headline agreement is misleading here. Then implement cohen_kappa(human, judge) and say what else you would report before relying on the judge.
a.answer:
Reconstruct the table. Humans: 90 ok, 10 bad. Judge: 95 ok, 5 bad. Agreement is 91, so let both-ok = a, both-bad = d. Human-ok-judge-bad = 90 - a, human-bad-judge-ok = 10 - d. Judge ok = a + 10 - d = 95 and a + d = 91 give a = 88, d = 3. So: both ok 88, human ok / judge bad 2, human bad / judge ok 7, both bad 3.

Observed agreement is 0.91. Chance agreement, given the marginals, is 0.90 x 0.95 + 0.10 x 0.05 = 0.86. Kappa = (0.91 - 0.86) / (1 - 0.86) = about 0.36. Most of the 91% is what two raters would reach by both saying 'ok' nearly all the time.

The more important number is per-class: of the 10 answers humans called bad, the judge flagged only 3 (30% recall on the class a faithfulness gate exists to catch), and of its 5 'bad' flags, 3 were right (60% precision). A gate with that profile lets about 7 in 10 unfaithful answers through.

Contrast: with balanced labels (50 ok / 50 bad) and the same 91% raw agreement, for example 46 / 4 / 5 / 45, kappa is 0.82. Same headline, very different reliability.

What to report: the confusion matrix, per-class precision and recall (or sensitivity and specificity), kappa with an interval (n = 100 with only 10 bad examples is very noisy, so oversample bad answers when building the calibration set), and human-human agreement on a subset, since the judge cannot be expected to beat the humans' own consistency. Kappa itself has quirks: it depends on prevalence and is not comparable across datasets with different class mixes. Re-check the judge when the prompt, the judge model, or the answer distribution changes.

b.q: You want to use an LLM judge to label support answers as 'acceptable' or 'not acceptable'. On 150 answers that a human reviewer also labelled, the counts are: both acceptable 120, judge acceptable but human not 10, judge not acceptable but human acceptable 5, both not acceptable 15. The vendor says '90% agreement, so it's good enough'. Evaluate that claim, state how you would calibrate the judge, and say how to treat the two kinds of labels honestly.
b.answer:
Raw agreement is 135/150 = 90%, but it is a weak summary here because the classes are imbalanced: the judge accepts 130 of 150 answers and the human accepts 125. A judge that always said 'acceptable' would agree with this human 125/150, about 83%, so 90% is less impressive than it sounds. Chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's kappa) is about 0.61, 'moderate to substantial', depending on the scale you use. More important for use are error-type rates: of the 25 answers humans rejected, the judge accepted 10 (40%). If the judge is used as a quality gate, 40% of bad answers slip through; its recall for unacceptable answers is 60% (15/25).

Calibration procedure.
1. Write the rubric with concrete criteria and examples of borderline cases; have two humans label independently on a sample and measure human-human agreement. That is the realistic ceiling; if humans agree only 85% of the time, a judge at 90% to one of them is not meaningful on its own.
2. Compare the judge with the human consensus on a sample that over-represents the rare class (bad answers), since 25 negatives give a very wide interval for judge recall.
3. Study disagreements by category (the 15 off-diagonal cases plus more): length preference, missed unsupported claims, leniency toward fluent text, rubric ambiguity. Revise the rubric or add a structured step (list claims, check each against the source), then re-measure on a fresh sample, not the one used for tuning.
4. Pick an operating point from costs: if a bad answer is costly, require a stricter threshold, use a second judge or a human check on borderline scores.
5. Monitor drift: re-audit a random sample of judged items regularly and whenever the judge model or prompt changes.

Honest labelling: the human labels are the reference but are themselves noisy and subjective; the judge's labels are model predictions (AI labels), and any dataset or metric built on them should say so and carry the measured error rates.

b.q: Answers are fluent and confident, but spot checks show many sentences are not in any retrieved chunk. Some are true, some are wrong. 'Unsupported' is a property of claim versus context; the causes differ in where the claim came from, so the first step is to measure support at claim level, then run tests that vary the context.

Step 1: split answers into atomic claims and label each as supported, contradicted or not found in the provided context (human labels on a sample, or a calibrated entailment judge). This gives the unsupported-claim rate, and shows whether unsupported claims are mostly true (suggesting parametric knowledge or sensible inference) or mostly wrong (confabulation or over-generalisation).

Step 2: closed-book test. Ask the same questions with no retrieved context. If the unsupported claims in the RAG answer reappear in the closed-book answer, they come from the model's parametric knowledge. Fix: stronger instructions to answer only from context, a requirement to cite per claim, an abstain option, and possibly a verifier that removes unsupported claims.

Step 3: relevance test. Measure whether the retrieved chunks actually contain the answer (context recall against a labelled answer span, or a manual check of 30 cases). If answer-bearing text is absent, the model fills gaps because the question cannot be answered from its context; the fix is retrieval, plus abstention when evidence is weak.

Step 4: over-generalisation test. When the answer-bearing text is present but the output states more than it says (a rule extended to all regions, a number rounded or merged), check the claim against the cited quote. Fix: quote-first prompting, lower generation temperature (helps variability, not the cause), and a verifier step.

The metrics to report are faithfulness (claims supported by context) separately from correctness (claims true), because the two diverge in exactly this scenario.

a.q: In a hybrid search system, a teammate computes final_score = bm25_score + cosine_score for each candidate and sorts. In testing, BM25 values look like 14.2, 9.8 and 3.1, while cosine scores are 0.71, 0.69 and 0.64 for the same documents. Why is this wrong, and what are the options for combining the two retrievers properly, with their trade-offs?
a.answer:
The two scores live on different, incomparable scales. BM25 is unbounded, depends on the query (its length and the idf of its terms) and on the corpus statistics, so a value like 14 for one query is not comparable to 14 for another. Cosine similarity is bounded in [-1, 1] and, for many encoders, concentrated in a narrow band, so differences of 0.02 can matter. Adding them means BM25 decides almost everything (differences of several points against hundredths), so the 'hybrid' is just BM25 with noise. The numbers above are illustrative.

Options: (1) Reciprocal rank fusion: score = sum over retrievers of 1 / (k + rank). It uses ranks only and needs no score calibration, which makes it a safe default (though some studies find a tuned convex combination beats it and that RRF is sensitive to its parameters), but it throws away score margins (a runaway winner counts the same as a near-tie) and depends on list depth. (2) Normalise then weight: min-max or z-score per query over the candidate list, then alpha x dense + (1 - alpha) x sparse. It keeps magnitudes and allows tuning alpha on labelled data, but min-max is sensitive to outliers and to candidate-list size, and a document missing from one list needs a defined fill value. (3) Learn a fusion or re-ranking model (for example a cross-encoder or a small learning-to-rank model using both scores as features) over the union of candidates; the most accurate option when you have labels, with more cost and maintenance. (4) Convert scores to calibrated relevance probabilities per retriever on labelled data, then combine.

Good default: start with RRF for robustness, then test a tuned weighted combination on held-out queries and keep it only if it wins consistently.

b.q:
A hybrid search service runs BM25 and dense retrieval across 8 shards. Each shard computes BM25 with its own local statistics, returns its top 20, and the coordinator merges the lists by raw score and then fuses with the dense list. After the corpus was resharded unevenly, queries with rare terms started returning odd rankings, and the hybrid scores seem on a different scale than the dense ones.

Why does this happen, and how should the merging and fusion work?
b.answer:
Why raw merging fails: BM25 weights terms by IDF, computed from document frequency and collection size. Using the common Lucene-style form idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)), a term that appears in 5 of 250,000 documents on one shard has idf of about 10.72, while on another shard where it appears in 40 of 250,000 it has about 8.73. For the same term frequency and document length, the first shard produces larger scores. Merging by raw score then favours shards where the term happens to be locally rare, a bias that grows with uneven resharding (for example one shard holding a topical cluster). When the corpus was split randomly, local statistics approximate the global ones for common terms and the problem is usually small (very rare terms stay noisy even then); after skewed resharding it is not.

Fixes: (1) compute or distribute global term statistics (a first pass collects document frequencies from all shards, or a periodically refreshed global dictionary), at the cost of an extra round trip or stale stats; many distributed search engines support such a mode. (2) Route documents so each shard is a statistically fair sample of the corpus. (3) Avoid relying on raw cross-shard BM25 scores: per-query score normalisation or merging by per-shard rank are only fallbacks, because both remain unsafe when shards differ in size or content, so prefer global statistics or even routing.

Hybrid fusion: BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus-dependent; cosine similarities lie in [-1, 1] and often cluster in a narrow band. Adding them directly gives one signal dominance. Reciprocal rank fusion scores a document as the sum of 1 / (c + rank) over lists (c = 60 is a widely used default), which needs no calibration: a document ranked 1st in BM25 and 3rd in dense gets 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.03227, just above one ranked 2nd in both (2/62 = 0.03226), so the two are nearly tied: RRF rewards a top rank only slightly more than consistent agreement. The alternative is min-max or z-score normalisation per list, which is sensitive to outliers and list length, plus a tuned weight.

Candidate depth: each shard must return at least the number of candidates you want globally (to guarantee an exact merged top-k each shard must return k), and for fusion take more than the final k from each retriever (for example 50 to 100 for a final 10) because a document ranked 30th in one list may be 2nd in the other. a.q: An email-and-web agent can read web pages, read the user's inbox and send email. Explain, in terms of the agent's control flow, why a web page that the agent merely 'reads' can end up causing the agent to send mail to an outside address, and what design rule would limit the damage without removing the web tool.
a.answer:
Control-flow view. The loop is: model reads context, emits a tool call, the runtime executes it, the result is appended, repeat. Untrusted content (a web page, an email body, a file) enters at the 'append result' step and is then processed by the same model, with the same authority to choose the next call, as the user's request. The research on indirect prompt injection describes this as LLM-integrated applications blurring the line between data and instructions, with injected text in retrieved data able to influence how and whether other tools or APIs are called. The model is trained to follow instructions in text, and instruction-like text inside a page is still text in its context; there is no dependable in-band marker that the model will always honour as 'this is only data'.

Why the damage is possible: it needs three ingredients together. (1) Exposure to untrusted content (the web tool). (2) Access to sensitive data (the inbox). (3) An outward channel (send email, or a call whose arguments reach an attacker). With all three in one session, a successful steering of the model can move data out. Removing the web tool removes the feature, so cut a different leg.

Design rules.
- Treat the session as tainted after untrusted content enters; after that point, tools that read private data or communicate externally are disabled or need explicit user confirmation showing the exact recipient and content.
- Split roles: a quarantined sub-agent reads untrusted pages and returns only a constrained, validated summary (fixed schema, no free-form instructions), while the privileged agent that can send mail never sees the raw page.
- Fix recipients from an allowlist or the user's own address book; arguments are validated by code.
- Least privilege per task: a 'summarise this page' task gets no send tool at all.
Honest limit: filtering prompts for suspicious phrases is unreliable, since attackers can phrase injections in endless ways; structural limits on what a compromised model can do are more dependable, though they cost usability.

b.q: A data-analyst assistant is given three tools: run_sql, read_file and send_report_email. The team plans to use one service account with broad access for all users because 'the prompt tells the model to stay within the user's data'. How would you scope permissions properly?
b.answer:
Do not make the prompt the access-control layer. The model's behaviour is probabilistic and can be influenced by user text and by anything it reads, so every permission must be enforced by the tools and the systems behind them, as if the model were an untrusted client that might emit any call.

Concrete design:
- Act as the user, not as a superuser. Pass the end user's identity or a scoped token derived from it to the tool, so the database applies that user's row-level and table permissions. A single broad service account turns any steering of the model into access to everyone's data (a confused-deputy problem).
- Least privilege per tool. run_sql uses a read-only role limited to the needed schemas; deny DDL and writes at the database level; add statement timeouts, row limits and cost limits. read_file is confined to an allowed directory with path normalisation to block traversal. send_report_email may only send to the user's own address or an approved domain list, with attachments produced by the system.
- Per-task tool set. A request to 'explain this query result' needs no email tool; grant tools for the task at hand rather than everything always.
- Validate arguments in code, independently of the schema shown to the model: parse SQL or use parameterised, pre-approved query templates for sensitive tables; check recipient addresses; reject unexpected arguments.
- Rate limits and quotas per user and per session, to bound the damage of a runaway or hijacked loop.
- Confirmation for outward or irreversible effects (email with data), showing the exact recipient and content.
- Audit log tying every call to the user, session and prompt version, with alerting on unusual volume.
- Secrets never in the prompt or tool output.

Trade-offs: finer scoping means more engineering and sometimes refused legitimate queries; start with the highest-impact controls (user-scoped read-only data access and a recipient allowlist) and expand. No scoping removes all risk, but it bounds what a mistaken or manipulated model can do.

a.q:
A RAG bot is asked: 'How many days of notice are needed to cancel the contract?' The retriever returns only a superseded policy page saying 30 days (the current policy says 60). Three candidate answers:

A: 'You need 30 days of notice.'
B: 'You need 60 days of notice.' (no retrieved text mentions 60)
C: 'Cancellations must be made in writing and follow the contract terms.'

For each answer say whether it is faithful, relevant and correct, state which inputs each of those three judgements needs, and explain what this implies for choosing the headline metric of a RAG evaluation.
a.answer:
Faithfulness (groundedness): are the claims in the answer supported by the retrieved context? Inputs: answer and context only. Answer relevance: does the answer address the question asked? Inputs: question and answer. Correctness: does it match the truth? Inputs: a reference answer or an authoritative source.

A: faithful (30 days is in the context), relevant, incorrect. The generator did its job; the failure is upstream, in retrieval or in index freshness (a superseded document outranked or replaced the current one). Faithfulness scoring alone would give this answer full marks.

B: unfaithful (60 is not in the retrieved text), relevant, correct. Perhaps the model recalled it from pre-training or guessed. It looks good on a correctness metric but is untrustworthy: on another question the same behaviour yields confident fabrications. A strict grounded-answer product would count this as a failure even though the user got the right number.

C: only loosely relevant (on-topic but non-responsive) and not correct. Its faithfulness depends on text we are not shown: if the retrieved page really says cancellations must be in writing under the contract terms it is faithful, otherwise it is unsupported too. When supported, it is the typical 'safe vague' answer that high faithfulness scores reward. Relevance and correctness catch it.

Implications: no single number is enough. Faithfulness guards against unsupported claims but not against bad context; correctness needs labelled references, which are expensive and go stale when policies change; relevance is cheap but weak. Report them together and read the pattern: low faithfulness points at generation (prompting, decoding, instruction to abstain), faithful-but-wrong points at retrieval, freshness or the corpus, and relevant-but-vague points at prompt or answer-format issues. Also check context relevance/recall separately, since an LLM judge of faithfulness inherits any errors in the context it is shown.

b.q: Answers are fluent and confident, but spot checks show many sentences are not in any retrieved chunk. Some are true, some are wrong. How do you determine whether the model is drawing on its own training knowledge, over-generalising from the chunks, or being fed irrelevant context, and what does each finding imply for the fix?
b.answer:
'Unsupported' is a property of claim versus context; the causes differ in where the claim came from, so the first step is to measure support at claim level, then run tests that vary the context.

Step 1: split answers into atomic claims and label each as supported, contradicted or not found in the provided context (human labels on a sample, or a calibrated entailment judge). This gives the unsupported-claim rate, and shows whether unsupported claims are mostly true (suggesting parametric knowledge or sensible inference) or mostly wrong (confabulation or over-generalisation).

Step 2: closed-book test. Ask the same questions with no retrieved context. If the unsupported claims in the RAG answer reappear in the closed-book answer, they come from the model's parametric knowledge. Fix: stronger instructions to answer only from context, a requirement to cite per claim, an abstain option, and possibly a verifier that removes unsupported claims.

Step 3: relevance test. Measure whether the retrieved chunks actually contain the answer (context recall against a labelled answer span, or a manual check of 30 cases). If answer-bearing text is absent, the model fills gaps because the question cannot be answered from its context; the fix is retrieval, plus abstention when evidence is weak.

Step 4: over-generalisation test. When the answer-bearing text is present but the output states more than it says (a rule extended to all regions, a number rounded or merged), check the claim against the cited quote. Fix: quote-first prompting, lower generation temperature (helps variability, not the cause), and a verifier step.

Interpretation caution: a true but unsupported claim is still a policy risk when the system promises answers 'from the documents', and the correct fraction does not make the system faithful. The metrics to report are faithfulness (claims supported by context) separately from correctness (claims true), because the two diverge in exactly this scenario.

a.q: Product wants to test a redesigned checkout button on a site with about 40,000 eligible visitors per day and a 4.0 percent checkout conversion. Design the experiment: primary and guardrail metrics, randomisation unit, sample size and duration, novelty effects, and the stopping rule.
a.answer:
Primary metric: checkout conversion, defined precisely as users with at least one completed order divided by users exposed, over a fixed window after first exposure. Guardrails: revenue per user and average order value, payment failures, page load time, refund/cancel rate, and error rate; the test should not ship if a guardrail degrades beyond a pre-agreed margin even when conversion rises.

Randomisation unit: the user (stable cookie or account id), not the page view, so each person always sees one version and the analysis unit matches the randomisation unit. If many users share devices or switch between logged-out and logged-in, consider the logged-in id where available. Check sample ratio mismatch (an observed split deviating from 50/50) before reading results; it signals an assignment or logging bug.

Sample size: to detect a 5 percent relative lift (4.0 to 4.2 percent) at two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80 percent power, the standard two-proportion formula gives roughly 154,000 users per arm (normal approximation, equal allocation; computed). A 10 percent relative lift (4.0 to 4.4 percent) needs about 39,500 per arm. The minimum detectable effect should be set by what is worth shipping, not by what is convenient.

Duration: at 40,000 visitors a day (about 20,000 per arm) about 154,000 per arm takes roughly 8 days if every daily visitor were a new unique user; in practice longer, so run two full weeks to cover complete weekly cycles, since weekday and weekend behaviour differ. Note that repeat visitors mean unique users accumulate more slowly than visits.

Novelty effect: a new button may get extra clicks simply for being new, or lose in the short run through change aversion. Look at the effect by day and by new versus returning users, and run long enough to see it settle.

Stopping rule: fix sample size, duration and the analysis in advance (pre-registration). Do not stop when p first dips below 0.05; repeated peeking inflates false positives unless you use a sequential method designed for it.

b.q: A marketplace tests a new ranking model with a 50/50 split. One engineer wants to randomise each request; another wants to hash the user ID. The 'recommended for you' carousel shows a +6% click lift in week 1 that decays to +1.5% by week 3. Compare the two ways of splitting traffic for consistency and interference, explain the decay, and say what you would put in place.
b.answer:
Per-request randomisation gives many independent assignments and the highest statistical power for request-level outcomes (for example, 'was this impression clicked'), but each user sees both models. The experience is inconsistent, and outcomes that accumulate over a user (retention, repeat purchase, trust) are blended across arms, so they cannot be attributed to either model. It suits stateless, memoryless situations such as a latency or error comparison.

Hashing the user ID (with an experiment-specific salt, so assignments are not correlated with other concurrent tests) gives sticky assignment: a user always sees the same model, user-level metrics are interpretable, and the same user cannot learn from one arm and act in the other. Cost: fewer independent units, and analysis must treat users, not requests, as the unit. Verify the split is balanced with a sample-ratio check; a deviation from 50/50 beyond chance indicates an assignment or logging bug.

Neither method fixes interference. In a marketplace, arms compete for shared inventory, shared caches or a model that retrains on logged feedback from both arms, so one arm's gains can come at the other's expense and the measured difference is not what a full rollout would give. Where interference is likely, consider randomising by cluster (market, region, seller group) or alternating whole-system time blocks (switchback), and watch for effects on shared resources.

The decay from +6% to +1.5% is consistent with a novelty effect: users click on something that looks different, then adapt. Other explanations exist (a differing mix of new and returning users, seasonality, or a feedback loop), so I would: run long enough for the effect to stabilise; report the metric by week and by new versus returning users; use holdout users who keep the old model for the longer term; decide on the stabilised effect; and avoid shipping on early lift.

a.q:
A team hosting a decoder-only model wants a small capacity-planning helper. Write two functions.

kv_cache_bytes(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_elem=2) returns the bytes needed to cache keys and values for `batch` sequences of `seq_len` tokens.

max_concurrent_sequences(total_bytes, weight_bytes, reserve_bytes, n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, bytes_per_elem=2) returns how many full-length sequences fit after subtracting the weights and a fixed reserve (activations, runtime overhead) from the device memory. It returns 0 if not even one fits, and raises ValueError if weights plus reserve already exceed total memory.

Validate inputs: every size must be an int (bool and float rejected with TypeError) and positive (ValueError); reserve_bytes may be 0. Then, for a hypothetical 32-layer model with head_dim 128, 4,096-token sequences, an fp16 cache, an 80 GiB device, 14e9 bytes of weights and a 6 GiB reserve, report how many sequences fit with 32 KV heads versus 8 KV heads, and what that tells you about the design of the attention layer.
a.answer:
The cache stores one key vector and one value vector per layer, per KV head, per token, so bytes = 2 x n_layers x n_kv_heads x head_dim x seq_len x batch x bytes_per_elem. It is linear in every factor, which is why, for a model this size with long contexts and large batches, the cache rather than the weights is what exhausts memory.

For the hypothetical model: per token the cache is 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 bytes (0.5 MiB) with 32 KV heads, so a 4,096-token sequence needs exactly 2 GiB. With 8 KV heads it is 128 KiB per token and 512 MiB per sequence.

Capacity: usable = 80 GiB - 14e9 bytes (about 13.04 GiB) - 6 GiB, roughly 60.96 GiB. Floor division by 2 GiB gives 30 sequences with 32 KV heads; dividing by 512 MiB gives 121 with 8 KV heads. At 1,024 tokens the 8-head model would hold 487.

What it tells you: the number of KV heads is a direct lever on concurrency. Multi-query and grouped-query attention share each key/value head across several query heads, which shrinks the cache and, per the GQA paper, is aimed at faster decoder inference while staying close to multi-head quality after uptraining. The trade-off is an architectural choice that must be made at training (or uptraining) time, and quality should be checked.

Pitfalls: the formula is an optimistic estimate. Real servers also lose memory to fragmentation, to activations, and to allocation granularity, and they may share prefix blocks between requests, so treat the result as a planning bound. Also state your units (GiB vs GB) and the cache dtype, which can differ from the weight dtype.

b.q: On a hypothetical accelerator with 300 TFLOP/s of usable fp16 compute and 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth, you serve a 7B-parameter fp16 model (14 GB of weights) with 32 layers, 32 KV heads and head_dim 128. A colleague says: "Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, so just keep growing the decode batch until the GPU is saturated." Using a back-of-envelope roofline, show why batch-1 decode is bandwidth-bound, how far batching really helps with 2,000-token contexts, and what the numbers say about prefill.
b.answer:
Ridge point: 300e12 FLOP/s / 2e12 B/s = 150 FLOP per byte. A kernel below that intensity is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.

Batch-1 decode: each new token costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter, so 2 x 7e9 = 1.4e10 FLOP, while every weight (14e9 bytes) must be streamed from memory. Intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte. Time is at least 14e9 / 2e12 = 7 ms per token (about 143 tokens/s), whereas the arithmetic needs only 1.4e10 / 3e14, roughly 0.05 ms. The compute units are almost idle.

Batching helps because the same weight read serves B sequences: weight intensity grows roughly as B, reaching the ridge near B = 150 if weights were the only traffic. But each sequence also has its own cache. At 0.5 MiB per token (2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 bytes), a 2,000-token context is about 1.05e9 bytes, read on every step. Step time is then at least (14e9 + B x 1.05e9) / 2e12: B = 1 gives 7.5 ms (about 133 tokens/s), B = 16 gives 15.4 ms (about 1,040 tokens/s), B = 64 gives 40.6 ms (about 1,580 tokens/s). Compute at B = 64 is only about 3 ms, so the step is still bandwidth-bound, and throughput approaches a ceiling of 2e12 / 1.05e9, about 1,900 tokens/s. (B = 64 also needs about 67 GB of cache on top of 14 GB of weights, so device memory capacity may cap the batch first.) Per-token latency also grows with B.

Prefill of the 2,000-token prompt costs about 2 x 7e9 x 2,000 = 2.8e13 FLOP, around 93 ms at peak, while the weights are read once for all 2,000 tokens: intensity of about 2,000 FLOP/byte (2.8e13 FLOP over 1.4e10 weight bytes, ignoring attention and activations), well above the ridge of 150, so compute-bound. Prefill therefore dominates time to first token and decode dominates inter-token latency.

Consequences: fewer KV heads, a lower-precision cache, or shorter contexts raise the batching ceiling; the exact numbers are idealised and real kernels reach only a fraction of peak.

a.q: Implement psi(reference, current, n_bins=10, eps=1e-4) with numpy only. Bin edges must come from quantiles of the reference sample, current values outside the reference range must still be counted, and empty bins must not produce log(0) or a division by zero. Then explain why a PSI computed from 200 reference rows, 200 current rows and 40 bins is a poor drift signal even when nothing has changed.
a.answer:
Design choices. Quantile edges taken from the reference give roughly equal reference mass per bin, which copes with skewed features; the edges are frozen so every later window is compared on the same bins. np.unique collapses duplicate edges, so a feature with a large spike (say many zeros) simply ends up with fewer bins. If only one or two distinct edges survive (a constant, or a binary feature so imbalanced that the interpolated quantiles stay at 0 and 1; a 50/50 binary feature keeps an interior edge at 0.5) there are no interior edges, so the code falls back to one bin per distinct value plus open bins on both sides; otherwise any change would score 0. Searching only the interior edges sends values below the reference minimum to the first bin and values above its maximum to the last, so out-of-range data is counted rather than dropped. Proportions are floored at eps because (q - p) * log(q / p) is undefined when either proportion is 0.

The floor makes the output an artefact once a bin is empty. With a 20,000-row N(0,1) reference and 1,000 current values all equal to 5.0, the PSI was about 12.4 with eps=1e-6 and about 3.9 with eps=1e-2. Read such a value as 'enormous', not as a magnitude to compare across runs.

Why 200 rows and 40 bins is a bad signal: PSI is a sum over bins of sampling noise even without drift. A rough chi-square-style argument gives an expected null value near (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m): for B=10 and n=m=200 that is 0.09, and a 300-repetition simulation with two samples from the same normal distribution gave a mean of 0.089 (sd 0.046). With 40 bins (about 5 expected rows per bin) the approximation breaks down and the simulated mean was 0.50 (sd 0.15). Commonly quoted rule-of-thumb cutoffs such as 0.1 and 0.25 are not statistical thresholds, and with 40 bins both would be exceeded in nearly every run with no change at all (a 2,000-run check gave 98% above 0.25). Remedies: fewer bins, more rows, a longer window, or calibrating the alert threshold against the noise floor measured on same-distribution splits.

b.q: On Monday 06:10 the drift job pages you: txn_amount has PSI 8.3 against the training reference, and the model's score distribution has collapsed to near-constant high scores. The same report shows discount_pct at PSI 0.05, below the team's 0.1 'investigate' line, yet a colleague points out its null rate went from 0.2% to 9% on Friday after an upstream ETL release; downstream code imputes nulls with 0. Product's first instinct is to retrain. How do you triage, what do the two numbers tell you, and what changes in monitoring?
b.answer:
Do not retrain yet; treat both as data-quality incidents until proven otherwise.

txn_amount: a PSI of 8.3 means essentially all current values fall in bins that held little reference mass. A change of units by a large factor such as 100 does exactly that for a narrowly spread amount distribution; with a wider spread the PSI is lower (about 4 for a lognormal with sigma 2) but still far above any threshold. In a simulation (50,000 lognormal amounts each side), multiplying every value by 100, as dollars-to-cents would, gave PSI about 8.2 with 10 quantile bins and eps=1e-4 (the ceiling for that setup is about 8.3) while two plain samples gave about 0.0003 (lognormal with sigma 1). Real behavioural drift rarely multiplies every quantile by the same constant. Check: compare quantiles (p10, p50, p99) of current vs reference; a near-constant ratio such as 100 points to a unit or schema change. Then confirm in raw logs, the upstream release notes and the data contract, and look for a step at a deploy timestamp across all slices. The collapsed scores are most likely a consequence: the model is probably being fed out-of-support inputs (confirm by re-scoring a sample with the amounts rescaled). Fix at the source (or add an explicit conversion in the feature pipeline), backfill or mark the affected window, and exclude it from training data. Retraining on a mix of units would bake the bug into the model.

discount_pct: a null-to-zero spike moves about 9% of the mass into the lowest bin. In a simulation with a continuous discount_pct and no reference zeros, PSI was only about 0.055 with 10 bins (about 0.09 to 0.10 with 20); with 20% of the reference already at zero it was about 0.015 to 0.03 (depending on how the ties at zero are binned). At 10 bins all are under the 0.1 line (20 bins sit right at it), although the feature is broken. Binned distribution distances are weak at detecting a modest mass moving inside a single bin. Add explicit data-quality monitors measured before imputation: null rate, zero rate, min/max and unit-sanity bounds, schema and type checks, each with absolute bands from history. The ML Test Score paper lists matching data against a schema and alerting when it diverges as a monitoring test.

Routing: data-quality alerts go to the data owner and block automated retraining; distribution drift goes to the model owner.

a.q:
An experiment was configured for a 50/50 split. After a week the analysis table shows 50,000 users in control and 51,200 in treatment. A PM says "that's only 2.4% off, close enough".

Implement srm_check(counts, expected_ratios, alpha=0.001) -> (chi2, df, p_value, mismatch_flag), a chi-square goodness-of-fit test for sample ratio mismatch, with no scipy (use math.erfc for df = 1). Example: srm_check([50000, 51200], [1, 1]) should give chi2 about 14.23 with a very small p-value and a True flag. Then say how you would interpret this, which causes you would investigate first, and what you do with the experiment's results.
a.answer:
Treat it as a failed experiment until explained. Expected counts are 50,600 each, so chi2 = 2 * 600^2 / 50,600 = 14.23 with df = 1 and p = 1.6e-4. If assignment really were 50/50, a gap this large would be very unlikely: with 101,200 users, treatment has 2.4% more users than control (50.6% vs 49.4% of the total), far more than chance allows. SRM alarms commonly use a very low threshold such as 0.001 (a convention, not a law), and this still trips it.

```python
import math

def srm_check(counts, expected_ratios, alpha=0.001):
    """Chi-square goodness-of-fit for sample ratio mismatch.
    counts: observed users per arm; expected_ratios: intended allocation (any
    positive weights). Returns (chi2, df, p_value, mismatch_flag).
    Raises ValueError for mismatched lengths, fewer than two arms, negative,
    NaN or infinite counts, non-positive ratios, or an all-zero total."""
    if len(counts) != len(expected_ratios) or len(counts) < 2:
        raise ValueError("need matching counts and ratios for at least 2 arms")
    if any(not math.isfinite(c) or c < 0 for c in counts) or any(
            not math.isfinite(r) or r <= 0 for r in expected_ratios):
        raise ValueError("counts must be finite and >= 0, ratios finite and > 0")
    total = sum(counts)
    if total <= 0:
        raise ValueError("need at least one observed user")
    ratio_sum = sum(expected_ratios)
    expected = [total * r / ratio_sum for r in expected_ratios]
    chi2 = sum((o - e) ** 2 / e for o, e in zip(counts, expected))
    df = len(counts) - 1
    if df == 1:
        # chi-square(1) survival function: P(Z^2 > x) = erfc(sqrt(x/2))
        p_value = math.erfc(math.sqrt(chi2 / 2))
    else:
        # Even/odd closed forms of the chi-square survival function
        x = chi2 / 2
        if df % 2 == 0:
            p_value = math.exp(-x) * sum(x ** k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(df // 2))
        else:
            p_value = math.erfc(math.sqrt(x)) + math.exp(-x) * sum(
                x ** (k + 0.5) / math.gamma(k + 1.5) for k in range(df // 2))
    return chi2, df, p_value, p_value < alpha
```

For df = 1 the chi-square survival function is erfc(sqrt(chi2 / 2)). The closed forms for other degrees of freedom make it work for multi-arm tests (values for 1 to 5 degrees of freedom agree with scipy.stats.chisquare). b.q: An A/B test of a new ranking model (planned 50/50 by user hash) reports +3.1% conversion for treatment. A reviewer notices that assignment counts are 51,000 vs 49,000 users out of 100,000, and that the serving stack has (a) a result cache keyed by (query, locale) with a 10-minute TTL and (b) an online-learning component that updates one shared set of item-popularity weights from clicks in both arms. Explain what each of these can do to the experiment, how you would test for them, and how you would fix the setup.
b.answer:
Two separate problems show up in the description.

1. Sample ratio mismatch (SRM). With 100,000 users and a 50/50 plan, you expect 50,000 per arm. The chi-square statistic for 51,000 vs 49,000 is (1000^2/50000) x 2 = 40.0 on 1 degree of freedom, and the p-value is about 2.5e-10 (computed). Chance does not explain that, so something in the pipeline treats the arms differently: for example a crash, redirect, bot filter or logging loss that affects one arm, or assignment happening after an event that differs by arm. Do not interpret the +3.1% until the SRM is explained, because the missing users are rarely missing at random.

2. Interference between arms. The result cache keyed only by (query, locale) means whichever arm populates an entry first determines what the other arm's users receive for 10 minutes, so some control users see treatment rankings and vice versa. The shared online-learning weights mean treatment clicks update the model that also serves control, so the two arms are no longer independent systems; the test then measures a blend, which typically biases the estimated difference towards zero (direction is not guaranteed, for example when the learner favours the arm that generates more clicks). This is the stable-unit-treatment-value problem seen from the operations side. Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems notes that a model may directly influence the selection of its own future training data; an online learner shared across arms is a version of that.

Fixes: include the experiment arm in the cache key (or bypass caching for the test); keep separate learner state per arm, or freeze learning during the test and compare fixed models; log both the assigned and the actually served variant per request and analyse by served arm only as a diagnostic; run an A/A test through the same stack to see whether the pipeline produces SRM or a non-zero difference with identical arms.

a.q: You are building training data for a churn model. Feature rows are (entity, feature_ts, value) and labelled events are (entity, event_ts). A colleague joins each event to the newest feature row per entity and gets a surprisingly high validation score. Explain what is wrong, then implement point_in_time_join(events, feature_rows, ttl) returning, for each event, the latest value with feature_ts <= event_ts and event_ts - feature_ts <= ttl, else None. Say how you treat ties on feature_ts.
a.answer:
The colleague's join uses information from the future. A label event at time t should be paired with the feature values that were known at t, but the 'newest row per entity' includes updates made after t, for example a ticket count that already reflects the complaint that preceded the churn. The model then learns from signals that cannot exist at prediction time, so validation looks better than production will. This is temporal leakage, and it also creates skew, because the live system by construction can only see the past.

A point-in-time (as-of) join fixes this by selecting, per event, the most recent feature row with feature_ts <= event_ts. Feast documents this behaviour as joining features onto an entity dataframe in a point-in-time correct way, reproducing the state at each entity timestamp, and also scanning backward from that timestamp up to a TTL. The TTL bounds staleness: a feature last updated a year ago should usually not be treated as current, so beyond the TTL the value is missing (None), mirroring what a serving system that treats old values as expired would return.

Implementation notes. Group rows by entity and sort by timestamp, then use binary search (bisect_right on the timestamps) to find the last row not after the event; that is O(log n) per event after an O(n log n) sort. The comparison must be less-or-equal on the timestamp: a row stamped exactly at the event time was available then. In the tests, with TTL 300, an event at 250 sees the value written at 200, an event at 800 sees nothing because the newest row (t=400) is 400 s old, and the naive join returns the t=400 value for every u1 event, including the one at t=99 where nothing was yet known. Ties: when two rows share a timestamp, I let the one appearing later in the input win, which is a convention you must make deterministic and document; in practice a separate ingestion or created-at timestamp is a better tie-breaker. One more subtlety: feature_ts here is the time the value was true; if data arrives late, you also need the time it became known (see backfill questions).

b.q: Your training data is stored as training_rows(row_id, entity_id, prediction_ts, label_ts) plus a long table training_features(row_id, feature, feature_ts) in which feature_ts says when each feature value was computed. A nightly snapshot job and a join on calendar date are suspected of leaking future information. Write one SQLite query that lists, per feature, how many training rows use a value computed after the row's prediction time, the share of rows, the worst case in hours ahead, and how many of those values are even later than the label time, returning only offending features. Then interpret the result on a small example and say what the query cannot catch.
b.answer:
The test is a per-row comparison of two timestamps: a feature value is point-in-time correct for a training row only if it was computed at or before the moment the prediction would have been made (prediction_ts). Grouping by feature turns that into an audit that shows which feature is the problem and how bad it is. Comparing feature_ts with label_ts (assuming label_ts is never earlier than prediction_ts, so rows_after_label is a subset of rows_from_future) separates two different failures: a value that is later than prediction_ts but earlier than the label is a point-in-time violation (the live system could not have known it), while a value later than label_ts may be derived from the outcome itself, which is target leakage proper.

On the example run (SQLite dialect, executed in the test on 4 training rows and 12 feature values, where refund_flag is stamped between 12 hours and about 20 days after prediction time and days_since_login is stamped 23:59 on the prediction day for three of the four rows): refund_flag has all 4 rows from the future, up to 470 hours ahead, and all 4 are after the label time, so it is almost certainly computed from the outcome and should be removed or rebuilt. days_since_login has 3 of 4 rows (share 0.75) from the future by at most 15 hours and none after the label: it is a nightly snapshot stamped at the end of the day and joined by date, so it leaks a few hours of future activity; the fix is an as-of join (latest value with feature_ts <= prediction_ts) or a snapshot taken before prediction time. orders_30d does not appear because every value precedes its prediction time.

Limits. The query trusts feature_ts. If the stamp is the event time rather than the time the data was actually available, late-arriving records still leak (the failure in a backfill over records that arrived days late). Features with no timestamp, rows whose label_ts is NULL (they are never counted in rows_after_label), leakage that is not temporal (duplicate entities across train and validation, aggregates computed over the full dataset), and clock or timezone mixing are not caught. ISO-8601 text compares correctly as strings only if every value uses the same format and timezone.

a.q:
A 32-layer decoder has hidden size 4096. In every layer you attach LoRA adapters with rank r=8 and alpha=16 to the q_proj and v_proj weights only, each a 4096 x 4096 matrix.

(a) How many trainable parameters does this add, and how does that compare with fully fine-tuning those same 64 matrices?
(b) Write lora_param_counts(d_out, d_in, r) -> (lora_params, full_params, ratio), lora_forward(x, W, A, B, alpha, r) for the unmerged path y = x W^T + (alpha/r) (x A^T) B^T, and merge_lora(W, A, B, alpha, r) returning W + (alpha/r) B A. W is (d_out, d_in), A is (r, d_in), B is (d_out, r). Show with numpy that merged and unmerged outputs agree and that the update has rank <= r.
(c) Why is B initialised to zero, what does alpha/r do, and when might LoRA be a poor choice?

Example: lora_param_counts(4096, 4096, 8) -> (65536, 16777216, 0.00390625).
a.answer:
(a) One adapter on a 4096 x 4096 matrix has A (8 x 4096) and B (4096 x 8): 8 * (4096 + 4096) = 65,536 parameters versus 16,777,216 for the full matrix, i.e. 0.39%. Over 32 layers x 2 matrices that is 4,194,304 (about 4.2M) trainable parameters versus 1,073,741,824 (about 1.07B) for those matrices fully fine-tuned. The count is r(d_in + d_out), linear in r, against d_in * d_out.

(b) LoRA freezes W and learns a low-rank update delta W = (alpha/r) B A. Because matrix multiplication is associative and linear, x (W + s B A)^T = x W^T + s (x A^T) B^T, so the merged weight gives the same outputs (up to floating-point error) with no extra inference latency, and the update has rank at most r even though W is full rank. Demonstration:
```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d_out, d_in, r, alpha = 12, 20, 4, 8
W = rng.normal(size=(d_out, d_in)); A = rng.normal(size=(r, d_in)) * 0.1; B = rng.normal(size=(d_out, r)) * 0.1
x = rng.normal(size=(5, d_in))
Wm = merge_lora(W, A, B, alpha, r)
assert np.allclose(x @ Wm.T, lora_forward(x, W, A, B, alpha, r), atol=1e-10)
assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(Wm - W, tol=1e-9) == r  # <= r in general; == r for random A, B
```

```python
import numpy as np

def lora_param_counts(d_out, d_in, r):
    """Trainable parameters of one LoRA adapter vs. full fine-tuning of that weight (no bias)."""
    lora = r * (d_in + d_out)          # A: (r, d_in), B: (d_out, r)
    full = d_out * d_in
    return lora, full, lora / full

def lora_forward(x, W, A, B, alpha, r):
    """Unmerged path: y = x W^T + (alpha/r) * (x A^T) B^T.  x: (n, d_in), W: (d_out, d_in)."""
    return x @ W.T + (alpha / r) * (x @ A.T) @ B.T

def merge_lora(W, A, B, alpha, r):
    """Merged weight W' = W + (alpha/r) * B @ A, same shape as W."""
    return W + (alpha / r) * (B @ A)
```

(c) B starts at zero (A random) so delta W = 0 and training starts exactly from the pretrained model; if both were zero no gradient would reach either factor, and if both were large the start point would be perturbed. alpha/r is a constant scale on the update; it lets you change r without retuning the learning rate as much, though how well that holds is empirical.

Limits (hedged): memory savings are smaller than the parameter ratio suggests, because activations must still be stored and the frozen base still has to be loaded; you do save gradients and optimiser state for the frozen weights. The original LoRA work reports quality close to full fine-tuning on several tasks, but this is task-depend

b.q: Your team can LoRA fine-tune a mid-sized decoder on two GPUs, but only one is available this quarter, and someone suggests QLoRA. Describe what QLoRA changes relative to plain LoRA, what you give up, and what you would verify before shipping an adapter trained that way.
b.answer:
Plain LoRA freezes the base weights, usually held in 16-bit, and trains low-rank adapter matrices, so optimiser state and gradients exist only for the small adapters. QLoRA goes one step further: the frozen base is stored in a 4-bit quantised format, and gradients flow through it into the adapters (Dettmers et al. also introduce a 4-bit data type tuned for normally distributed weights, quantisation of the quantisation constants, and paged optimiser states to absorb memory spikes). During the forward and backward pass, weight blocks are dequantised to a higher-precision compute type as they are needed, and adapters stay in higher precision.

What you gain: the dominant fixed cost, the base weights, shrinks by roughly a factor of four relative to 16-bit, which is why a model that needed two GPUs may fit on one. The authors report that task performance matched 16-bit fine-tuning in their experiments; treat that as evidence about their setups, not a guarantee for yours.

What you give up. Activation memory (which grows with batch size and sequence length) is not reduced by quantising weights, so long sequences can still run out of memory unless you also use gradient checkpointing or shorter sequences. Dequantisation adds compute, so steps are often slower than LoRA with a 16-bit base on hardware where that fits. Quantisation introduces approximation error in the frozen weights, which the adapter partly absorbs during training but which can hurt on sensitive tasks.

Before shipping: evaluate on your held-out task and on general-behaviour regressions; decide the serving form up front. If you serve with the same quantised base, evaluate that. If you merge the adapter into a 16-bit base, the weights differ from what training saw, so re-evaluate the merged model rather than assuming equivalence.

a.q: You must pick an ANN index for 50 million 768-d float32 chunk embeddings. Constraints: about 1 million new chunks per day plus a few thousand deletions, a target of roughly 0.95 recall@10 against exact search, p95 latency under 50 ms, and 64 GB of RAM per node. Compare HNSW, IVF-Flat and IVF-PQ (with and without re-ranking from full vectors) on recall, latency, memory, build cost and update behaviour, and say which you would shortlist and why.
a.answer:
Sizing first: 50M x 768 x 4 B = 153.6 GB for raw float32, so a single 64 GB node cannot hold flat vectors in any index; you either shard, compress, or keep full vectors on disk.

HNSW: a layered proximity graph. At high recall it is often among the lowest-latency options (the best choice depends on data and recall target), and it supports incremental inserts. Costs: graph links on top of the vectors (memory grows with M), a build time that rises with efConstruction, random memory access that wants everything in RAM, and deletes that are often implemented as tombstones (implementation-dependent), so heavy churn degrades quality until a rebuild. Recall/latency is tuned at query time via efSearch.

IVF-Flat: a k-means coarse quantiser splits vectors into nlist cells; a query scans nprobe cells. Training is a one-off step on a sample, adding is cheap (assign to the nearest centroid), deletes are easy, and recall/latency is tuned with nprobe. Memory is still the full vectors. Its weakness is that the centroids are trained on a snapshot of the data, so they go stale if the content distribution shifts.

IVF-PQ: vectors are stored as short product-quantised codes (for example 96 bytes instead of 3072). Distances are approximate, so recall has a ceiling set by quantisation error, often well below the flat variant at equal nprobe. The standard remedy is to fetch a short list (say the top 100-200 by PQ distance) and re-rank with full vectors from SSD or memory-mapped storage; this restores most of the lost recall at the cost of extra I/O.

Updates at 1M/day (about 12 per second on average) are easy for IVF and feasible for HNSW; the deletions are few, so tombstones plus a periodic rebuild are acceptable.

My shortlist: IVF-PQ with re-rank (fits the memory budget), and as an alternative HNSW over sharded or compressed vectors if the latency budget is tight. I would not choose by reputation; I would build both on a 2-5M sample, compute recall against exact search, and plot recall versus p95 latency.

b.q: Your team says the new vector index 'has 98% recall' but nobody can say how that was measured. Describe how to measure ANN recall@k properly, then implement it: write exact_topk(queries, base, k) (brute-force L2 ground truth), ann_recall_at_k(exact_ids, approx_ids) (mean overlap fraction, ignoring -1 padding) and a small inverted-file index ToyIVF(base, nlist, seed) with search(queries, k, nprobe). Show how recall changes with nprobe and what happens when nprobe equals nlist.
b.answer:
ANN recall@k is the average fraction of the true k nearest neighbours (found by exact search under the same metric) that the approximate index returns. Procedure: sample queries that look like production traffic, not a random subset of the indexed vectors (a vector queried against an index containing itself is trivially found); compute exact top-k by brute force on the same data; run the ANN index at a given parameter setting (nprobe, efSearch); average |exact ∩ approx| / k over queries. Report it together with latency, as a curve over the search parameter, because a single recall figure without the setting is meaningless.

Details that matter: ground truth and index must use the same metric and the same normalisation; ties in distance can make the 'true' top-k ambiguous (set-overlap is slightly pessimistic or optimistic in that case); k must match the k you serve; padding (-1) from an index that returned fewer than k hits must count as misses, not be dropped from the denominator. ANN recall is not task recall: an index with ANN recall 0.95 can still be fine for the task if the missed neighbours were marginal, and 100% ANN recall cannot repair a poor embedding model.

IVF logic: a k-means coarse quantiser partitions the base into nlist cells; a query finds its nprobe nearest centroids and exactly ranks only the vectors in those cells. Because the candidate set grows with nprobe and the final ranking inside it is exact, recall is non-decreasing in nprobe (barring exact distance ties at the k-th place) and equals 1.0 when nprobe = nlist (it degenerates to brute force). The speed gain comes from scanning roughly nprobe/nlist of the data when cells are balanced.
